title: Abraha's elephant
hookLine: the Yemeni ruler's army marches on Mecca, and Abd al-Muttalib says the House has a Lord who will protect it (Surah 105)
tomorrow: a name no one had heard

cards: An elephant kneels in the dust outside Mecca and will not get up. Its handlers beat it, the sirah says, then turn it toward Yemen, and it rises and walks. Turn it back toward Mecca, and down it goes again.

Behind it waits an army, come to tear down the Ka'ba. In front of it, a town that has mostly fled to the hills. And somewhere between the two, a grandfather who has just asked a king for something nobody expected.

teach.b: Abraha ruled Yemen, and the sirah says he wanted the pilgrims who went to Mecca to come instead to a great church he had built. So he marched north with an army and an elephant.
On the way, his men seized the camels grazing around Mecca, among them Abd al-Muttalib's. So the grandfather went to see the king. Abraha, the sirah says, was struck by him, and asked what he wanted.
My camels, he said. Abraha was taken aback. I have come to destroy the House that is your religion and your fathers' religion, and you speak to me of camels?
And Abd al-Muttalib answered with the line this story turns on: I am the lord of the camels. The House has a Lord who will protect it.
Then he went home, told the Meccans to take to the hills, and, the sirah says, held the door of the Ka'ba and prayed. The Qur'an tells what happened next in the surah called the Elephant.
Pickthall translates: "Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant?"
Did He not bring their plan to nothing, the surah goes on, and send against them "swarms of flying creatures", pelting them with stones of baked clay, and leave them like a field eaten bare?
The Arabic there is ababil, and Pickthall renders it swarms. The surah never names what kind of creature they were.
Years later, at Hudaybiyah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was riding his camel, al-Qaswa, toward Mecca, and she knelt and would not move.

teach.h: THE HOUSE HAS A LORD WHO WILL PROTECT IT.
teach.b: People said she had turned stubborn. No, he said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: she isn't stubborn. She was held back by the One who held back the elephant.

how: Surah al-Fil, the Elephant, is short enough to be taught to children and recited in the daily prayers, and the story of Abraha is told in sirah classes as the prelude to the Prophet's birth.

o: a white elephant given as a gift to Quraysh
the animal the Prophet rode at Hudaybiyah
the army that marched on Mecca and was turned back

s: the surah names the species of the ababil
Pickthall renders ababil as swarms; the surah never names their kind.
Abd al-Muttalib asked Abraha for his camels back
and said the House has a Lord who will protect it.
the Prophet mentioned the elephant at Hudaybiyah
his camel was held back, he said, by the One who held back the elephant.

games.q: you're Abd al-Muttalib. a king with an army has come to destroy the House, and his men have taken your camels. you're granted an audience. what do you ask for?
o: let Mecca pay you to leave.
games.why: the sirah says he asked for his camels: I am the lord of the camels. the House has a Lord who will protect it.

practice: Name one thing you've been guarding with all your strength, a plan, a child's future, a reputation, and for a few breaths do what Abd al-Muttalib did: look after your own camels, the part that really is yours, and loosen your grip on the rest.
If you pray, you can hand the rest to Allah in your own words; if you don't, simply notice how much of it was never in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Abraha's elephant. The army that marched on Mecca, the elephant that knelt, and a grandfather's answer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the house has a lord. Tomorrow, a name no one had heard. Day seven hundred five.

sources.q: Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant?

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2731 (al-Qaswa held back by the One who held back the elephant)
